source_refs.note: Exercise 2.1, Question 13 (i)-(ii): dy/dx for parametric equations; book p. 41. Unit 2 has no printed answers.

blocks.prompt: 13 (i) Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) for the following parametric equations: \(x = \sin^2 t\) and \(y = \cos 2t\)
blocks.explanation:
Parametric equations: \(x\) and \(y\) are both given in terms of a parameter \(t\).
Use \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\) (section 2.3.2).
Plan: differentiate each w.r.t. \(t\), divide, simplify with \(2\sin t\cos t = \sin 2t\).
steps:
Given: \(x = \sin^2 t\), \(y = \cos 2t\).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
Method: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), provided \(\frac{dx}{dt} \neq 0\).

Differentiate x w.r.t. t
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2\sin t\cos t = \sin 2t\]
Why: chain rule on \((\sin t)^2\); double-angle formula.

Differentiate y w.r.t. t
\[\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -\sin 2t \cdot 2 = -2\sin 2t\]
Why: chain rule on \(\cos(2t)\).

Divide
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{-2\sin 2t}{\sin 2t} = -2\]
Why: parametric formula; valid where \(\sin 2t \neq 0\).

Check by removing t
\[\cos 2t = 1 - 2\sin^2 t\]
\[y = 1 - 2x\]
Why: the curve is part of a straight line with slope \(-2\).

blocks.prompt: 13 (ii) Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) for the following parametric equations: \(x = \sqrt{1 + \sec t}\), and \(y = \sqrt{\tan t}\)
blocks.explanation:
Parametric again, now with square roots, so each \(t\)-derivative needs the chain rule.
Use \(\frac{d}{dt}\sqrt{w} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{w}}\cdot\frac{dw}{dt}\) for both.
Plan: find \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt}\), divide, then simplify using \(\frac{\sec t}{\tan t} = \csc t\).
steps:
Given: \(x = \sqrt{1 + \sec t}\), \(y = \sqrt{\tan t}\), with \(0 < t < \frac{\pi}{2}\) (where both roots are real and nonzero).
To find: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\).
Method: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\).

dx/dt
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{1 + \sec t}} \cdot \sec t\tan t\]
Why: chain rule, \(w = 1 + \sec t\), \(\frac{dw}{dt} = \sec t\tan t\).

dy/dt
\[\dfrac{dy}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\tan t}} \cdot \sec^2 t\]
Why: chain rule, \(w = \tan t\), \(\frac{dw}{dt} = \sec^2 t\).

Divide
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sec^2 t}{2\sqrt{\tan t}} \cdot \dfrac{2\sqrt{1 + \sec t}}{\sec t\tan t}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sec t\sqrt{1 + \sec t}}{\tan t\sqrt{\tan t}}\]
Why: dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal; one \(\sec t\) and the 2s cancel.

A neater form
\[\dfrac{\sec t}{\tan t} = \csc t,\quad \dfrac{1 + \sec t}{\tan t} = \dfrac{1 + \cos t}{\sin t}\]
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \csc t\sqrt{\dfrac{1 + \cos t}{\sin t}}\]
Why: \(\frac{\sqrt{1 + \sec t}}{\sqrt{\tan t}} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + \sec t}{\tan t}}\) (both positive here); multiply top and bottom of \(\frac{1 + \sec t}{\tan t}\) by \(\cos t\).

Check at t = pi/4
\[\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{1 + 0.7071}{0.7071}} \approx 2.197\]
Why: both forms give the same number, and a numerical check with sympy agrees.
blocks.final_answer: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sec t\sqrt{1 + \sec t}}{\tan t\sqrt{\tan t}} = \csc t\sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos t}{\sin t}}\)
